value.overview: The Sanderling (Calidris alba) is a small, long-distance migratory shorebird that breeds in the high Arctic and spends the nonbreeding season on coasts around much of the world. It is especially recognizable for its rapid “wave-chasing” feeding style, running along the waterline as waves recede. In Costa Rica, it is a regular coastal migrant and winter visitor, occurring on both the Pacific and Caribbean shores, particularly where suitable sandy or muddy intertidal habitat remains.
value.classification: The Sanderling belongs to the sandpiper family Scolopacidae and the shorebird order Charadriiformes. It is one of the smaller species in the genus Calidris.
value.identification: A Sanderling is a compact, short-legged sandpiper about 18–20 cm long, with a straight, fairly stout black bill and black legs. Nonbreeding adults are very pale gray and white, with a clean breast and a dark shoulder area that may be faint. Breeding plumage is more reddish-brown on the head and upperparts. In flight, it shows a strong white wing stripe. Unlike most small sandpipers, it lacks a hind toe. Its distinctive behavior is running quickly at the edge of breaking waves.
value.rangeHabitat: Sanderlings breed across high-Arctic tundra in North America, Greenland, and Eurasia, then migrate south to coastal regions worldwide. During migration and winter they use sandy beaches, exposed tidal flats, mudflats, estuaries, lagoons, salt ponds, and occasionally rocky shores. In Costa Rica, they occur along both the Pacific and Caribbean coasts. They are common during migration, especially from about mid-August through October and from mid-March into early May, and are less common but widely distributed during the winter season. They are not known to breed in Costa Rica.
value.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant. Birds seen in Costa Rica are mainly southbound migrants, winter visitors, and northbound migrants. Costa Rican records indicate peak passage from mid-August–October and mid-March–early May, with some individuals remaining through the winter; summer occurrence is not regularly reported.
value.breeding: Sanderlings breed in the high Arctic during the brief summer season. The nest is a shallow scrape on the ground, usually in an open, sparsely vegetated area such as a rocky ridge, slope, or slightly elevated patch of tundra near moist ground or ponds. The female typically lays a small clutch of eggs, and both adults may participate in incubation and care of the young. There is no reliable evidence that the species breeds in Costa Rica.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of small marine and terrestrial invertebrates, including insects, crustaceans, mollusks, worms, and other tiny shoreline organisms. On beaches, Sanderlings probe and pick prey from wet sand exposed by receding waves, often feeding at the surf edge. They also forage on mudflats, tidal flats, and coastal lagoons. In the Arctic, they take insects and other tundra invertebrates and may also consume some plant material.
value.behavior: Sanderlings are active, social birds that commonly feed and roost in flocks, sometimes alongside other shorebirds. Their rapid movement along the shoreline, synchronized with incoming and outgoing waves, is characteristic. Flocks may suddenly take flight when disturbed and relocate a short distance before resuming feeding. Individuals spend much of the day foraging, although some may defend small feeding areas, especially during migration or in places with concentrated food supplies.

conservation.populationTrend: Population trends vary geographically. Some long-term monitoring programs report declines, particularly among populations using the Americas, while other regional populations are stable or increasing. The overall global trend is not uniform, and changes may be difficult to detect because Sanderlings depend on widely separated breeding, stopover, and wintering sites.
conservation.threats: Important concerns include loss and alteration of sandy beaches, tidal flats, estuaries, and other coastal stopover or wintering habitats. Disturbance from recreation, coastal development, pollution, oil spills, and reduced food availability can affect birds concentrated along the shoreline. Because Sanderlings migrate across continents, impacts at several sites along their annual route may combine to reduce survival and breeding success.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore beaches, estuaries, tidal flats, and coastal wetlands used by shorebirds. Keep dogs under control and give feeding and roosting flocks plenty of space, especially during migration and winter. Prevent litter, oil, and chemical pollution from entering coastal habitats. Support protected coastal areas, responsible shoreline planning, and shorebird monitoring programs in Costa Rica and along the species’ broader migration routes.
